Returns: Choose how the app simulates returns. 'Random, from your assumptions' uses your projected numbers, 'Random 5-year blocks' shuffles real market stretches from 1928 to 2025, and 'Every historical start year' tests the plan from each past start date.
Trials: How many random simulations to run. More trials give a steadier picture of what might happen; 1,000 is a good default, and you can go up to 10,000 for finer detail.
Currency: The currency to display all dollar amounts in this view. If you live abroad and think in euros or pounds, pick that here so the numbers match your daily life.
Claim the foreign earned income exclusio: Check this if you work abroad and want to exclude up to the IRS limit of foreign-earned income from your US taxable income. This lowers the tax the plan projects on your earnings.
Yearly housing cost abroad (today's $): Enter your annual rent, utilities, and insurance costs while living abroad, in today's dollars. A portion between 16% and 30% of the exclusion limit is also tax-free under the foreign housing exclusion.
Plan currency: The currency all amounts in this plan are saved and shown in. If you live abroad and budget in a different currency, set it here; everything else converts to this.
From year: The year this line item (income, expense, or other) starts. For example, if you will receive a bonus beginning in 2027, enter 2027 here.
Plan name: A label for this plan so you can tell it apart from others. For example, '2025 Retirement Plan' or 'Post-Job-Change Scenario.'
First year: The starting year for the plan's projections. Enter the year you want the plan to begin, such as 2025 if you are planning from now.
Filing status: How you file your US federal income tax return. Pick 'Married filing jointly' if you and your spouse file together, 'Single' if you do not, or 'Head of household' if you support a dependent.
State: The US state where you live for tax purposes. State income and property taxes differ, so this affects the taxes the plan projects each year.
Name: This person's name in your plan. You can type any label you like, such as 'Alex' or 'My spouse.'
Birth year: The year this person was born. The app uses this to track their age and apply age-based tax rules, like when retirement account withdrawals become mandatory.
Plan to age: The age the plan projects this person will live to. A common starting point is 85 or 90; the plan models spending and savings up to that age.
Retirement age: The age at which this person plans to stop working and draw from retirement accounts. For example, enter 65 if you expect to retire at 65.
Type: What kind of account this is, such as a 401(k), traditional IRA, Roth IRA, or a regular taxable brokerage account. The type determines how withdrawals are taxed.
Owner: Which person in the plan this account belongs to. If you and a spouse each have separate accounts, assign the right person here.
Cost basis: The total amount you originally paid for the investments in this taxable account. The app uses this to figure out how much of a sale is taxable profit versus your original money.
Stocks: The percentage of this account you want in stocks (equities). This affects how much the account can grow and how much it can swing up or down.
Bonds: The percentage of this account in bonds (government or corporate debt). Bonds are generally steadier than stocks but pay lower returns.
Cash: The percentage of this account held in cash or near-cash (money-market funds, savings). Cash is safe but earns very little and loses value to inflation.
Yearly fee: The percentage the account charges you each year for management. For example, a 0.25% fee on a $100,000 account costs $250 per year.
Its own yearly return, not the market mi: Check this if this account earns a return separate from your overall stock-and-bond mix, such as a fixed annuity. Leave it off to let the account follow your general allocation.
Yearly return (after fees): Enter the yearly percentage this account is expected to earn, after its own fees. For example, a 4% fixed annuity would be entered as 4.
Return tied to inflation (Series I bonds: Check this if the account's return rises with inflation, like Series I savings bonds or TIPS. The app adds the yearly inflation rate to a small fixed rate.
Fixed rate above inflation: The small fixed percentage added on top of inflation for this account. For example, if a bond earns 1% above inflation each year, enter 1.
Pay dividends and interest out to cash (: Check this for a taxable account where dividends and interest are paid to you in cash instead of being automatically reinvested. This changes how the account grows and how you are taxed each year.
Foreign tax withheld on dividends: The percentage of dividends a foreign government withholds before they reach you. For example, if Canada withholds 15%, enter 15. This can offset US taxes via the foreign tax credit.
Real estate (property tax, deductible mo: Check this to mark the account as a real estate holding. The app will then project property tax and let you claim deductible mortgage interest.
Yearly appreciation: The percentage you expect the property's value to increase each year. A typical starting point is 3%, but it varies by location and market.
Yearly rent, if rented (today's $): The total rent you expect to collect each year from tenants, in today's dollars. Enter 0 if the property will not be rented.
Vacancy: The percentage of time you expect the rental unit to sit empty with no tenant. A common assumption is 5%, meaning about 6 weeks per year.
Rental costs (share of rent): The share of rent that goes to ongoing costs like maintenance, property management, and insurance. A typical starting point is 35%.
Sale year (0 for none): The year you plan to sell the property. Enter 0 if you do not expect to sell during the plan. A sale triggers capital gains tax on any appreciation.
Cost basis: price paid plus improvements: Enter what you originally paid for the property plus the cost of major improvements. The sale gain is the sale price minus this number, taxed at long-term capital gains rates.
Selling costs (share of the price): The percentage of the sale price that goes to agent commissions, closing costs, and pre-sale repairs. A typical figure is 6% to 8%.
The home you live in (its sale excludes: Check this if this is the home you actually live in. When you sell, the IRS lets each person exclude up to $250,000 of profit from capital gains tax, so a married couple can exclude $500,000.
Interest rate: The yearly interest rate on this loan, as a percent. For example, a 6.5% mortgage would be entered as 6.5.
Yearly payment: The total amount paid toward this loan each year, in today's dollars, covering both principal and interest. For a $300,000, 30-year mortgage at 6%, this is about $22,861.
Extra payment a year (today's $): Any extra amount you plan to pay toward the loan each year beyond the regular payment. For example, an extra $1,000 a year shortens the loan and saves interest.
Forgiven in year (0 for none): Enter the year a student loan will be forgiven, for example through Public Service Loan Forgiveness. Put 0 if the loan will not be forgiven.
Secured by: Pick the asset that backs this loan, such as your house for a mortgage. Choose Nothing if the loan is not tied to any asset.
Foreign income tax paid on it: Enter the percentage of income tax a foreign country takes from this income. As a US taxpayer, you receive a foreign tax credit for this amount on your return.
Earned while living abroad (a US person): Check this if you earned the income while living in another country. It changes how much US tax you owe on that money.
US Social Security and Medicare tax stil: Check this if your employer is a US company. Even while you live abroad, the 7.65% payroll tax (Social Security and Medicare) may still be withheld.
Real growth a year: Enter the yearly percentage this value rises above inflation. For example, 5% means it grows 5% more than prices do each year.
Start year: The calendar year this income or expense begins. For example, enter 2025 if you start a new job in 2025.
End year (0: at retirement or death): The year this income or expense stops. Enter 0 if it continues until you retire or pass away.
Keeps pace with inflation: Check this if the amount grows each year to match rising prices, such as a salary with annual cost-of-living raises.
Taxable: Check this if you owe income tax on this amount. Leave it unchecked for tax-free money, such as qualified Roth withdrawals.
Amounts in future dollars of their year: Check this if the amounts you enter are in the dollars of the year they occur, not today's dollars. For example, you might enter $100,000 as a 2035 salary rather than converting it to today's value.
A specified service business (law, healt: Check this if your self-employment is in law, medicine, consulting, or a similar profession. It changes how the qualified business income tax deduction works.
Health insurance premium a year (today's: Enter your yearly health insurance premium in today's dollars. As a self-employed person, you can deduct this amount up to your business profit.
Solo 401(k) deferral (share of profit): Enter the share of your profit you contribute to a solo 401(k) as an employee. For example, 10% means you set aside 10 cents of every dollar of profit.
Employer contribution: SEP IRA or solo 4: Enter the share of your net earnings that goes into a SEP IRA or solo 401(k) as an employer contribution. For a sole owner, the cap is 20%.
Vests over (years): Enter how many years it takes for all your RSU shares to become fully yours. For example, 4 means one-fourth vests each year over four years.
Cliff (years before the first vesting): Enter the waiting period before any shares vest. With a 1-year cliff on a 4-year schedule, nothing vests in year 1 and a quarter vests in year 2.
401(k) contribution: Enter the percentage of your salary you contribute to your 401(k). For example, 6 means you set aside 6% of each paycheck.
Share of the contribution going to Roth: Enter what portion of your 401(k) contribution goes to the Roth side, where qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. 100% means all Roth.
Yearly bonus (share of salary): Enter your bonus as a percentage of your salary. For example, 15 means your bonus equals 15% of your pay each year.
Employer match rate: Enter how much your employer adds for each dollar you contribute. For example, 50 means your employer adds 50 cents for every dollar you put in.
Match up to (share of pay): Enter the maximum share of your pay up to which your employer matches. For example, 5% means the match stops once you have contributed 5% of your salary.
Benefit at 67, monthly: Enter your monthly Social Security benefit at full retirement age (67). You can find this figure on your SSA statement at ssa.gov/myaccount.
Claim age (62 to 70): Enter the age you plan to start collecting Social Security. Waiting past 67 raises your monthly benefit, while claiming at 62 lowers it permanently.
Discretionary share: Enter the share of this expense you could cut if times got tough. The Strategy tool uses it to find savings during a bad market stretch.
End year (0: for life): Enter the year this expense stops. Put 0 if it continues for as long as you live, such as a subscription you keep indefinitely.
Growth above inflation: Enter the yearly percentage this amount rises beyond inflation. For example, 3% means it grows 3% more than the general price level each year.
Paid from: Pick the account or fund that will pay for this education expense, such as a 529 plan or your savings account.
Event: Choose the type of life event, such as buying a home, a child, or a career break. The form updates to show the fields relevant to that event.
Year: Enter the calendar year this event happens. For example, 2027 for a home purchase you plan in 2027.
Price (today's $): Enter the purchase price of the home in today's dollars, before any future inflation adjustment. For example, 450000 for a $450,000 house.
Down payment: Enter the share of the home price you pay upfront, as a percentage. For example, 20 means you put down 20% and finance the remaining 80%.
Closing costs: Enter closing costs as a share of the home price. Typical closing costs run about 2% to 5% of the purchase price.
Mortgage rate: Enter the yearly interest rate on your mortgage loan. For example, 6.5 means you pay 6.5% interest per year on the balance you owe.
Term (years): Enter the number of years over which you will repay the mortgage. Common terms are 15 or 30 years.
Yearly cost to 18 (today's $): Enter the annual cost of raising this child until age 18, in today's dollars. Include food, clothing, activities, and other recurring expenses.
College a year (today's $): Enter the annual cost of college in today's dollars. For example, 25000 for a year of in-state tuition, room, and board.
College years: Enter how many years of college you expect. For example, 4 for a standard bachelor's degree or 2 for an associate degree.
Person: Select which person in the household this event applies to, such as a career break or pay change for a specific family member.
Back to work after: Enter the year the career break ends and this person returns to work. For example, 2028 if the break is two years starting in 2026.
Yearly rent (today's $): The rent you collect from your rental property each year, in today's dollars (not adjusted for inflation). For example, if your tenant pays $2,000 a month, enter 24000.
Costs (share of rent): What fraction of the rent goes to expenses like property tax, insurance, repairs, and management fees. For example, if half the rent covers upkeep, enter 50%.
New state: Pick the state you are moving to. This changes the income and sales tax rates the plan uses from that point on. For example, select Colorado if you are relocating there.
Amount (today's $): How much money you expect to inherit, in today's dollars. For example, if your parent's estate is about $400,000, enter 400000.
As an inherited IRA (10-year rule): Check this if the money you inherit is an IRA that must be emptied within 10 years under the SECURE Act. The plan will spread withdrawals across those 10 years.
Every (years): How many years apart each payment in this repeating schedule happens. For example, enter 2 for a bonus you receive every other year.
Last year: The final calendar year this repeating payment is expected. For example, enter 2045 for a child support obligation that ends that year.
Who leaves the plan: Select the person whose accounts and income are being removed in this separation. For example, choose your spouse's name if they are leaving the household.
Share of every account kept: The percentage of each investment account the person leaving keeps with them. For example, enter 50% if you are splitting all accounts equally.
Expenses from then on (× before): A multiplier applied to your yearly spending after the separation. For example, enter 0.6 if your living costs drop to 60% of what they were before.
Support paid a year (today's $): The yearly alimony or support payment you make after the separation, in today's dollars. For example, enter 30000 for a $2,500-a-month obligation.
Support for (years): How many years you expect to pay support after the separation. For example, enter 5 if the agreement runs for five years.
Pay from then on (× current): A multiplier applied to your income after this event. For example, enter 0.5 if your pay drops to half after leaving a job.
When: Choose what triggers this milestone: a specific year, an age, reaching financial independence, or hitting a net worth target.
Age: The age at which this milestone or condition applies. For example, enter 67 if it should trigger at your full retirement age.
Condition: Pick what must be true before the linked rule kicks in, such as a year, an age, or reaching a net worth level. For example, choose 'From an age' to act at 55.
Cash to keep on hand (today's $): How much liquid cash you want to hold as an emergency buffer, separate from your investments. For example, enter 20000 for about six months of expenses.
Traditional IRA a year: How much you contribute to a Traditional IRA each year, which reduces your taxable income. For example, enter 7000 for the 2024 limit.
Roth IRA a year: How much you contribute to a Roth IRA each year, using money you already paid tax on. For example, enter 7000 for the 2024 limit.
HSA a year: How much you put into a Health Savings Account each year. For example, enter 4150 for the 2024 family maximum.
Backdoor Roth (no income limit on the Ro: Check this if your income is too high for a direct Roth IRA and you use the backdoor method (contribute to a Traditional IRA, then convert). The plan ignores the Roth income cap.
Mega backdoor Roth a year: How much extra you put into a Roth 401(k) each year through a post-tax contribution that your employer converts. For example, enter 15000 if your plan allows it.
Leftover pay goes to: Choose what happens to income that is not used for expenses, tax, or scheduled contributions: send it to a taxable investment account or use it to pay off debt first.
Change the order from a later year: Turn on to use a different withdrawal order from a future year. For example, draw from taxable accounts first, then switch to tax-deferred accounts after age 73.
From the year: The calendar year when the new withdrawal order takes effect. For example, enter 2048 if you switch the draw order that year.
How to draw: Choose how the plan takes money out of your accounts: in the fixed order you listed, or in proportion to each account's current balance.
Shield withdrawals under: Cap your yearly withdrawals so total taxable income stays below a chosen tax bracket or Medicare/health-insurance threshold. For example, pick 'The 12% bracket' to avoid the 22% rate.
Realize gains in the 0% capital gains ba: Check this to sell investments each year up to the amount that would not trigger any capital gains tax, resetting your cost basis. For example, if the 0% band is $47,600 in 2024, the plan sells up to that much in gains.
Spending rule: Pick how the plan decides your yearly spending: use the plan's built-in expenses, a fixed percentage of your portfolio, or a guardrail that adjusts the rate over time.
Withdrawal rate: The percentage of your portfolio you withdraw each year. For example, enter 4% for the classic 4% rule on a $1,000,000 portfolio.
Safe withdrawal rate (FI test): The withdrawal rate the plan uses to test whether you are financially independent. A common starting point is 4%, but you can lower it for extra safety.
Count real assets (home equity) toward F: Check this to include the value of your home minus the mortgage when the plan checks whether you have hit financial independence or a net worth goal.
Flexible spending: cut discretionary spe: Turn on to automatically reduce optional spending (like travel or dining) when the market has a rough stretch, and restore it when things recover.
Cut when the portfolio is under its high: How far below its recent peak the portfolio must fall before spending gets cut. For example, enter 15% to start cutting when the portfolio is 15% below its high.
Share of discretionary spending cut: The portion of your optional spending to reduce when the cut triggers. For example, enter 50% to halve travel and dining costs.
Raise when the portfolio is above its st: How much the portfolio must grow above its starting value before optional spending gets a boost. For example, enter 25% to add back spending once the portfolio is 25% higher.
Raise of discretionary spending: The percentage of optional spending to add back when the portfolio recovers. For example, enter 20% to bump discretionary spending up by that share.
Give to charity from IRAs from 71 (quali: Check this to send required minimum distributions straight to charity after age 71, which does not count as taxable income to you. For example, the plan directs your RMD to a charity each year starting at 71.
Shift from stocks to bonds with age: Turn on to gradually move the investment mix from stocks to bonds as you get older, reducing market risk near and after retirement. For example, shift from 90% stocks at 45 to 50% stocks at 70.
From age: The age when the gradual shift from stocks to bonds begins. For example, enter 45 to start the glide path at 45.
To age: The age at which your investment mix has fully shifted from mostly stocks to mostly bonds or cash. Enter the age you want to be mostly safe, for example 70.
Stocks at the end: The percentage of your portfolio still in stocks when the shift from stocks to bonds or cash is complete. For example, 40 means 40% in stocks and 60% in bonds or cash at the target age.
Fill up to the bracket: How far into a higher tax bracket you are willing to go when converting traditional IRA money to a Roth. Pick the bracket ceiling you want to stay under, or 0 to skip automatic conversions.
To year: The last calendar year the app will automatically convert traditional IRA money to a Roth. Enter the year, for example 2045. The default is 30 years after the plan starts.
Convert in year: The calendar year for this one-time manual Roth conversion. Enter the year you plan to move a specific lump sum from a traditional account to a Roth, for example 2032.
72(t) SEPP withdrawals before 59½ (no pe: Turn this on if you will take a series of equal withdrawals from a 401(k) or IRA before age 59.5 under IRS rule 72(t) to avoid the 10% early-withdrawal penalty. The payments must continue until 59.5.
SEPP from year: The calendar year your 72(t) equal-withdrawal schedule begins. For example, 2028 if you retire at 55 and start taking penalty-free payments that year.
From: The account you are moving money out of. Pick the source account, such as a Traditional 401(k) or a Roth IRA.
To: The account that will receive the money. Pick the destination, such as a Traditional IRA or a Roth IRA.
Amount a year (today's $): How much money moves each year, in today's purchasing power. The app adjusts it for inflation in later years. For example, enter 5000 for $5,000 a year.
Local tax: The extra tax your city or state adds on top of federal and state income tax. Pick NYC for New York City resident brackets, a flat rate on wages, a flat rate on taxable income, or None.
Preset: A saved set of local-tax settings you can reuse. Pick a preset name, or leave it on Custom to enter the rate yourself.
Rate: The percentage used for the local tax. Enter it as a percent, for example 3.07 for New York City's top bracket rate, or 1.5 for a flat 1.5% on wages.
Itemize when it beats the standard deduc: Turn this on to let the app itemize your deductions (property tax, mortgage interest, charity) when the total exceeds the standard deduction. Otherwise it uses the standard deduction automatically.
Property tax (share of home value): The percentage of your home's value you pay in property tax each year. For example, 1.5 means your annual property tax equals 1.5% of what your house is worth.
Limit mortgage interest to the first $75: Turn this on to apply the current tax rule that only mortgage interest on the first $750,000 of home loans counts as a deduction. Leave it off if all your home debt is under that limit.
Home debt limit ($1,000,000 for loans fr: The maximum home loan amount whose interest you can deduct from your taxes. Enter 750,000 for most loans, or 1,000,000 if your mortgage was taken out before December 16, 2017.
Charitable giving a year (today's $): How much you give to charity each year, in today's dollars. The app scales it up for inflation in later years. For example, enter 2000 for $2,000 a year.
Medicare from 65, with income surcharges: Turn this on if you will enroll in Medicare at 65. The app includes the extra Part B and Part D premiums (called IRMAA) that apply when your income is above certain thresholds.
Part D premium a month before surcharges: The monthly cost of your Medicare Part D prescription drug plan before any income-based surcharges. For example, enter 42 for a $42-a-month plan.
Medigap or Advantage premium a person a: The monthly premium for a supplemental Medicare plan (Medigap or Medicare Advantage) per person, in today's dollars. For example, enter 180 for a $180-a-month Medigap plan.
ACA marketplace coverage from retirement: Turn this on if you will buy health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace between retirement and age 65. The app estimates your cost using the benchmark silver plan.
Benchmark silver premium a person a year: The annual cost of a second-tier silver health plan per person, before any government subsidies. The app uses this to estimate your marketplace insurance cost. For example, enter 7200.
Inflation: The average yearly rate you expect prices to rise. Enter a percent, for example 2.5 for a 2.5% yearly increase in the cost of living.
Stock return: The average yearly return you expect from a stock fund. Enter a percent, for example 7 for a 7% yearly gain. The app uses this to project portfolio growth over time.
Bond return: The average yearly return you expect from a bond fund. Enter a percent, for example 3 for a 3% yearly gain.
Cash return: The average yearly return you expect from cash or money-market accounts. Enter a percent, for example 1 for 1% a year.
Stock volatility: How much stock returns swing up and down from year to year, as a percent. A higher number means bigger swings. The U.S. stock market has historically been around 16 to 18%.
Bond volatility: How much bond returns swing from year to year, as a percent. Bonds are usually much steadier than stocks. A typical value is around 4 to 6%.
Stock-bond correlation: A number from -1 to +1 showing how stocks and bonds relate to each other. Negative means when one goes up the other tends to go down. A typical value is around -0.3.
Dividend yield: The percent of your stock value paid out as dividends each year, before capital gains. For example, 2 means a $10,000 stock position pays about $200 in dividends a year.
Qualified share of dividends: The percentage of your dividends taxed at the lower capital-gains rate instead of your regular income rate. Most U.S. stock funds are near 100%, so enter 100 unless you hold real-estate funds (REITs) or foreign stocks.
Social Security raises beside inflation: An extra (or negative) yearly percentage added to Social Security benefits beyond inflation. Enter 0 to keep them level with inflation, or -0.5 to assume they lose half a point a year.
Tax model: How the app calculates your yearly taxes. Pick United States rules for the full federal, state, and local tax code, or One flat rate for a single percentage on all income.
Flat rate: The single tax rate applied to all your income each year. Only appears when the tax model is set to flat. Enter a percent, for example 25 for 25%.
Stress test: a market crash: Turn this on to simulate a sudden stock-market crash at a specific year and see how it affects your plan. It helps you check whether you can survive a bad market without running out of money.
Crash year: The calendar year in which the simulated market crash hits. For example, 2030 if you want to see the effect of a crash 10 years from the plan start.
Stocks fall by: The percentage your stock portfolio drops in the simulated crash year. For example, 35 means stocks lose 35% of their value in one year, similar to the 2008 crash.
Heirs' income tax rate: The income tax rate your heirs will pay on money or assets they inherit from you. Enter a percent, for example 24 for the 24% federal bracket.
Heirs are: Who will inherit your assets after you die. This affects the estate and inheritance taxes the app estimates. Pick children or grandchildren, siblings, or others such as nieces or friends.
Number of heirs: How many people (spouse, children, other beneficiaries) will inherit your estate when you pass away. This is used on the estate planning page to estimate the amount each person would receive.
Find the strategy with: Pick the goal the app should optimize for: the biggest total amount left to your heirs, or the smallest total tax bill over your lifetime. Whichever you choose shapes the recommendation below.
Chart: Controls how the results graph looks. Lines show each account as a separate line, stacked areas or stacked bars show them layered on top of each other so you can see the total and each piece.
I am planning with a spouse or partner: Turn this on if you are planning retirement together. The app will then ask for both people's salaries, accounts, and benefits, and will combine them in its projections.
State you live in: Select your state so the app can apply the right income tax, property tax, and other state-level rules. Your choice changes the tax estimates and the final strategy.
Yearly salary: Your total pay before taxes, bonuses included. For example, if you make $85,000 a year, enter 85000. This drives how much you can contribute to retirement accounts each year.
Share saved in a 401(k) or similar: The percentage of each paycheck that goes into your 401(k), 403(b), or similar workplace plan. If you divert 10% of pay, enter 10. This is your contribution, not the employer's.
Employer match of each dollar: How much your employer adds for every dollar you contribute. Many jobs match 50 cents per dollar (enter 50) or match dollar for dollar (enter 100). If your employer does not match, enter 0.
Match applies up to this share of pay: The cap on the employer match. For example, if your employer matches 50% but only on the first 6% of your pay, enter 6. Beyond that share, no extra match is added.
Age you plan to stop working: The age at which you expect to retire and stop earning a salary. The app uses this to split your timeline into working years and retirement years.
Monthly Social Security at 67 (0 to esti: The monthly benefit you would receive if you started Social Security at full retirement age 67. If you do not know, enter 0 and the app will estimate it from your pay history.
Checking and savings: Total cash in your checking, savings, and money-market accounts combined. For example, $12,000 in savings plus $3,000 checking means enter 15000.
Taxable brokerage accounts: Total value of investments held in a regular (taxable) brokerage account, such as one at Fidelity or Schwab that is not a 401(k) or IRA. Enter the current market value.
Amount paid for those investments (0 if: The original amount you contributed to your taxable brokerage account, also called cost basis. This helps the app estimate capital gains tax if you sell. Enter 0 if you do not have the number handy.
Health savings account (HSA): Current balance in your HSA. An HSA is a savings account you can use for medical costs, and withdrawals in retirement are tax-free if used for qualifying expenses.
401(k), 403(b), and traditional IRA: Total balance in pre-tax retirement accounts. Contributions reduce your taxable income now, but withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income.
Roth 401(k) and Roth IRA: Total balance in after-tax retirement accounts. You already paid income tax on the contributions, so qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
I own my home: Check this box if you and your partner (or you alone) own a home. It reveals the home-value and mortgage fields so the app can include your housing in the net-worth picture.
Home value: What you believe your home is currently worth on the market. A recent appraisal or a Zillow-style estimate works. Enter 350000 for a $350,000 home.
Mortgage balance: How much principal is still owed on your home loan. Check your last mortgage statement for the current balance. If you have no mortgage, enter 0.
Mortgage interest rate: The annual interest rate on your home loan, as a percentage. Look at your mortgage note or monthly statement. For example, a 6.5% rate means enter 6.5.
Monthly payment (principal and interest): Your monthly mortgage payment for principal and interest only, not including property tax or insurance. Find it on your mortgage statement. For a $1,800 payment, enter 1800.
Other debts, total balance: Combined remaining balance on all non-mortgage debts: car loans, student loans, personal loans, and credit-card balances. Add them up and enter the total.
Average interest rate: The weighted average rate you pay across those other debts. A rough estimate is fine. If you have a car loan at 6% and student loans at 5%, and the balances are similar, enter about 5.5.
Monthly payments, total: Add up the minimum monthly payments for all your non-mortgage debts (car, student loans, credit cards, etc.). For example, a $350 car payment plus a $200 student loan means enter 550.
Yearly living expenses: The total amount you spend in a year on everything: housing, food, transportation, insurance, entertainment, and all other bills. Check your last 12 months of spending. For $60,000 a year, enter 60000.
Yearly Roth IRA contributions: How much you currently put into a Roth IRA each year outside of your workplace plan. For example, if you contribute $5,000 a year, enter 5000. Enter 0 if you do not contribute.
Yearly HSA contributions: How much you deposit into your HSA each year, combining your own contributions and any employer deposit. If you put in $3,000 a year, enter 3000. Enter 0 if you do not contribute.
